segments.text: Occupational English Test, Practice Test, Listening Test.
This test has three parts.
In each part you'll hear a number of different extracts.
At the start of each extract you'll hear this sound.
You'll have time to read the questions before you hear each extract and you'll hear each
extract once only.
Complete your answers as you listen.
At the end of the test, you'll have two minutes to check your answers.
Part A. In this part of the test, you'll hear two different extracts.
In each extract, a health professional is talking to a patient.
For questions 1 to 24, complete the notes with information you hear.
Now look at the notes for extract 1.
This is a benchmark education solutions sample test paper.
Extract 1 questions 1 to 12.
You hear a cardiologist talking to a patient referred for dizziness.
For questions 1 to 12, complete the notes with a word or short phrase. You now have 30 seconds to look at the notes.
Hello Mr. Thatch, it's nice to meet you. How are you today?
Um, okay, I guess. You can call me Jack by the way.
Okay, thanks Jack. So, you were referred by a doctor in the A&E for an episode of Dizziness.
Yes, and I still feel a bit unwell, even though it has been about an hour since the
dizziness began.
So, let's talk about your health recently.
How have you been feeling lately?
I was feeling quite well until about six months ago.
I have had a few falls, not often but enough to worry me.
I see.
When you have fallen, have you lost consciousness?
Yes, a couple of times.
And as I live alone, I don't know how long I've been out when I come to.
I've also grazed my knees a few times.
Okay, and have you also felt dizzy before?
Yes, sometimes I feel dizzy and have to sit down to avoid passing out.
This has happened a few times after I was doing some work outside, but it happened last week
when I was just sitting there.
How long does it generally take for the episode to pass?
I would say it takes about 10 to 15 minutes.
Hmm, you said you lived alone.
Has anybody been with you when you have had one of these episodes?
Most of the time no, but my granddaughter was with me once.
She got so worried that she called an ambulance.
She said I looked so pale she thought I was dead.
By the time they got me to the hospital I had completely recovered.
They told me I had a normal electrocardiogram and a normal chest X-ray and they discharged
me.
Okay, so I can see from the initial physical examination done in the ANE, you were pale
when you presented in the ANE.
No heart murmurs were detected.
Let me look at the ECG that was just done.
Erm, well, what are you thinking it might be?
Well, your loss of colour suggests a loss of cardiac output associated with arrhythmia,
which is a problem with the rate of rhythm of your heartbeat.
It means that your heart beats too quickly, too slowly, or within a regular pattern.
Yes, your most recent ECG is showing a complete heart block.
The episodes of loss of consciousness are what we call Stokes Adams attacks and are caused
by rapid heartbeat or tachyarithmia. You likely started out with a partial block, but now
it seems that you are in a stable, complete heart block.
Does that mean the blood in my heart isn't flowing? How is that possible?
No. A heart block is an abnormal heart rhythm that occurs when the electrical impulses that
tell your heart when to beat are delayed or blocked as they travel through the heart.
Oh no. And what is the treatment for that?
The treatment is the insertion of a pacemaker, which will help monitor and control your heartbeat.
With the pacemaker, if your heart rhythm is abnormal, the computer in the pacemaker will
direct a generator to send electrical pulses to the heart.
So you have to insert it in my chest?
Is that major surgery?
It does not require open heart surgery so it is not as serious as you might think.
In fact, most people go home within 24 hours.
This is a benchmark education solutions sample test paper.
Extract 2, questions 13 to 24.
you hear a GP talking with a patient complaining of lack of energy.
For questions 13-24, complete the notes with a word or short phrase.
You now have 30 seconds to look at the notes.
Hello Mrs. Halloway, it's nice to meet you here today.
Um, nice to see you too.
So I see here that you decided to make the appointment because of a lack of energy.
Can you tell me a bit more about that?
Yes, it's awful.
Over the past year and a half I think I have become increasingly tired.
I work as a solicitor and there have been a few times now where I have fallen asleep
in my office.
I have had to give up my weekly game of tennis because I am just too tired.
And it is absolutely impossible for me to stay awake past half past nine at night or
wake up before 7.30am.
also quite difficult for me to concentrate when I finally do get to the office.
So you had an episode of depression about 10 years ago related to the breakup of your
marriage. Are you currently experiencing any personal problems?
Um, no, not at all.
Any other physical symptoms like being constipated?
Um, now that you mention it, I have been a bit constipated. Also, I have put on a bit
of weight over the past year, about 6 kilograms I think. One thing I wanted to ask about is
the possibility of diabetes. My brother was diagnosed with type 1 diabetes at the age
of 13 and I know fatigue is a symptom of diabetes.
Let's take a look at your latest blood tests. So, your glucose levels are within a normal
range, so it isn't diabetes. Hmm, I see that your skin is a bit dry and it's also somewhat
flaky. Is that normal for you?
Um, no, not really. I've been trying to do something about it.
Okay, so fatigue is associated with quite a few possible diagnoses, but based on your
lab results which show anemia and hypercholesterolemia, which is an elevated amount of cholesterol
in the blood, and a few other factors such as your general description of how you have
been feeling, the appearance of your skin and your family history. My initial diagnosis
is hypothyroidism. Does it explain why I am so tired even after sleeping the whole night?
Yes, it might. But of the reason you may be feeling tired is sleep apnea, which is often
associated with hypothyroidism, and may contribute to daytime sleepiness and fatigue. It can
also explain the weight gain since that is also a feature of the condition.
Is it common?
Well, it does typically present in the fifth or sixth decade, and it is five times more
common in women than men.
And I meet both of those criteria.
Yes, depending on the cause of a condition, it may also be related to your family medical
history. Your brother has an auto-immune disease, diabetes, which makes you a more likely candidate
for one as well. And a common cause of hypothyroidism is autoimmune thyroiditis.
Well, what can I do about it?
Well, first we will have to confirm the diagnosis with thyroid function tests. If hypothyroidism
is confirmed that we will then need to determine the cause in order to decide on treats.
That is the end of part A. Now look at part B.
Part B. In this part of the test, you'll hear six different extracts. In each extract,
you'll hear people talking in a different healthcare setting. For questions 25 to 30,
choose the answer A, B or C, which fits best according to what you hear. You'll have time
to read each question before you listen. Complete your answers as you listen.
Now look at question 25. You hear a conversation between a GP and a patient about recurring diarrhea.
Now read the question. This is a benchmark education solutions sample test paper.
So, Mrs. Johnson, it seems that your diarrhea has not cleared up.
Erm, oh no.
I took the medicine you prescribed, but I am still having diarrhea.
I've lost quite a bit of weight as well.
I remember in your initial appointment you said that your diarrhea was watery, yellow
and foul smelling and that you were experiencing a loss of appetite and nausea.
Now along with this weight loss I am suspecting it is something else.
Where was it you travelled to recently?
Was it somewhere in Eastern Europe?
To Russia at St Petersburg.
Um, okay, so I think what you have is Giardiusus.
It is most common in the tropics but is also found in Russia.
Question 26.
You hear a physician in the A&E department talking with a patient presenting with abdominal
pain.
Now read the question.
So, Mrs Hardy, you're complaining of abdominal pain.
Yes, it won't go away and it has become more and more severe over the last day.
I'm also feeling nauseated and hot and cold.
You are probably dehydrated.
Have you had any surgeries in the past couple of years?
Yes, I was treated for an ulcer about five years ago.
Well, I can see that you are running a fever and that you are and that you attend it in
the right upper quadrant and epigastrium.
I'm going to order an abdominal x-ray and blood test to help us get a better look at
what might be causing your pain.
In the meantime, I'm going to put you on intravenous fluids to avoid dehydration.
27. You hear a ward briefing about a newly admitted patient. Now read the question.
Okay, so last night a 35 year old man was admitted after he presented in the emergency
department because of a rapid onset painful swollen right knee.
There is no history of trauma to the knee or previous joint problem, and there is no
history of significant medical illnesses.
Patient feels generally unwell and has noticed that his eyes are sore.
His initial examination of cardiovascular, respiratory, abdominal and neurological systems
was normal.
His right knee was swollen, hot and tender with limitation, inflection.
An x-ray showed soft tissue swelling around the joint.
No other joint appears to be affected.
Patient reported having recently travelled to Thailand on business.
The probable diagnosis is post-infective inflammatory mucositis and arthritis, likely
triggered by non-gonococcal urethritis.
I have ordered urethral swabs to exclude chlamidial and gonococcal infections to get
a cause for the urethritis, and possibly for the inflamed knee.
Question 28. You hit part of the training on communication between providers. Now read
the question.
I am here today to introduce a new role at our facility as well as discuss some of the
problems this new role is intended to deal with.
First of all, the new role is clinical nurse leader.
We are assigning a clinical nurse leader to micro units of around 12 beds throughout the
hospital.
The clinical nurse leader will primarily function as a liaison between physicians and patients,
well as a mentor to other nurses. As you will know, we have experienced a range of problems
stemming from poor communication between providers, so one of the main purposes of this role is
to get better information flowing faster so that decisions can be made more efficiently
and more effectively. We think this will result in patients having a better healthcare experience,
with fewer redundancies and in physicians having a better understanding of what happens to
a patient when another provider takes over. Some other policies we are.
Question 29. You hear a trainee doctor discussing stress with a senior GP. Now read the question.
Dr James, you have been a GP for 15 years, right?
Erm, yeah, that's correct. I've seen general practice change quite a bit in that time. There
is an increasing workload and pressure on general practice. So much so that many younger
GPs are choosing to work as low-income GPs or choosing to work abroad. I mean, the big
part of the problem is from the lack of physicians choosing to go into general practice.
I've heard quite a few GPs talk about their days getting busier and longer in order to
cope with increased demand, which obviously makes it incredibly difficult to juggle working
life and home life, especially if one wants to have children.
Hmmm, yes, 12 hour minimum working days have definitely become the norm, not the exception.
I'm of the opinion that the current state of general practice is completely...
So, Dr. Alex, I've already spent over an hour going through the list of patients for
this morning's diabetic clinic.
I'm trying to decide which patients can be seen by the nurse and which should be seen
by the GP.
Hmm, let me see if I can help with that.
I mean, we already have quite a busy day with the second year medical students coming
in, which is going to reduce the number of patients one of the doctors can see.
Yes, every day is a case of juggling priorities and complex needs.
That is definitely true. I also have at least an hour of reports and routine administration
with prescriptions waiting for me. I wish it were easier to get some temporary support
until our colleague on sabbatical comes back.
That is the end of part B. Now look at part C.
Part C. In this part of the test, you'll hear two different extracts. In each extract,
hear health professionals talking about aspects of their work. For questions 31 to 42, choose
the answer A, B or C, which fits best according to what you hear. Complete your answers as
you listen. Now look at extract 1.
Extract 1. Questions 31 to 36. You hear part of a presentation about a recent
report on podiatry education. You now have 90 seconds to read questions 31 to 36. This
is a benchmark education solution sample test paper.
[Unclear interval — replay the original audio.]
Hello everyone. Thank you very much for attending this session on Pediatry Education to empower
patients to self-care. The reason that this research was undertaken was due to the many
surveys that have reported a high number of people suffering from foot problems. For example,
one survey showed that 95% of people over the age of 75 reported having problems cutting
their toenails. Another survey found that 29% of people over the age of 65 reported experiencing
problems with thickenails and or skin problems. Many of the conditions that patients present
with, such as those just mentioned, could be safely and appropriately handled by the
patients themselves, if they had the confidence, skills and knowledge to do so.
Some of these and other foot problems have previously required NHS Pidiatry services,
so empowering patients or their carers to deal with their own minor foot problems like
nail care can reduce the burden on NHS Prodiatry services and in turn save money. This would
also allow NHS Prodiatry services to concentrate more care on those with the greatest need and
highest risks such as people with diabetic foot problems.
With that in mind, this project was designed to identify and train patients suitable for
for self-care so that they can be discharged from the service.
Patients suitable for self-care include those who do not have any high-risk medical or podiatric
needs, as well as those who are fit and able to provide their own foot care or who have
a family member or care able to provide it for them.
For this project, a system was designed to triage patients as high or low risk as they
enter what we call the empowerment pathway. Patients considered to be high risk had one
or more of the following. A history of non-traumatic amputation, foot infection or foot and ulcer
were on oral steroid therapy or had an infected ingrowing toenail among others. Examples of
conditions considered to be low risk were painful callus or corns or thickened and deformed
nails. Patients assessed as low risk or able to provide their own foot care safely were
discharged to self-care with advice as well as follow up awareness sessions. Awareness
sessions were provided in local health centres and up to 10 patients were invited to each.
In addition, invited patients were encouraged to bring a family member, carer or spouse
with them if they felt they were unable to carry out daily living activities for themselves.
The sessions covered the role of podiatrists, the type of conditions that are treated by
the NHS podiatry service and the types of common foot problems that can be self-managed.
Training was also provided to patients on safe nail filing and leaflets were provided
to reinforce the information.
If at this time patients revealed they had a more serious foot problem or medical condition,
they were offered an assessment by the podiatrist.
After the initial phase of the project, which included the triaging system and awareness
sessions just described, the first impact was noted in the first group of patients assessed.
The benefit for the NHS was a saving of over £138,000 for a population of £560,000.
This savings resulted from enabling some patients to be discharged from the podiatry service
to self-care.
If we look at it on an individual level, for every patient who can self-care, NHS saves
about £55 per year, which is the cost of a 40-minute assessment appointment conducted
by a qualified podiatrist. This project also helped to reduce the caseload of podiatrists,
who prior to the project had an average more patience than comparable services, like physiotherapy
and psychology. The benefit to patients with serious foot conditions was also quite dramatic,
Because before the project began, there was a waiting list of approximately 3 years due
to the lack of spare capacity and very few people being discharged from the case load.
Once this initiative was fully implemented, all high risk referrals were seen within 4
weeks and all low risk referrals were seen in 12 weeks.
And finally, for the patients involved in the project, patient satisfaction has been
improved because all patients were assessed by a podiatrist and given one to one foot
care advice. We have worked closely with patients, including conducting surveys and
one to one interviews, to examine how patients feel about the empowerment pathway. As a result,
We are working to make some changes to this initiative, which include.
Now look at Extract 2.
Extract 2.
Questions 37-42.
You hear an interview with a nurse about common problems in hospitals.
You now have 90 seconds to read questions 37 to 42.
[Unclear interval — replay the original audio.]
Hello everyone, I want to welcome you all today to this interview with the leader of
the Australian Nursing Federation. Sally began her career in nursing in aged care,
and she also has a background in oncology and emergency nursing, having held a variety
of roles. Her areas of interest are standards and practice, leadership and patient safety.
So, Sally, tell us about what originally attracted you to the field of nursing.
I always knew I wanted to do something in healthcare, but I think what drew me to nursing
was the fact that nurses are uniquely positioned as advocates for patients.
I liked the idea of working for and with patients to help in the planning and delivery of health services.
Mmm, that's an interesting take on things. So now in your role as president of the Australian
Nursing Federation, you work to promote and protect the profession.
Yes, that's what we do. I mean, it isn't just me. I work with a strong and experienced
team to improve the interests of nurses and midwives in the country.
So you're here today to talk about some of the challenges that nurses face in the hospital
setting.
So what, in your opinion, is one of the biggest challenges facing nurses in this setting?
Well, it is hard to say which is the biggest challenge, but one that we have been hearing
more about lately is the desire for physician integration in care teams.
We have more and more low-income physicians, which is good for the physicians because they
get the flexibility in terms of time and location.
But this means that there is a less of a chance for physicians to integrate with the
rest of the team. It also means that we the nurses are doing double duty because these
physicians don't communicate with the rest of the team very well. I mean I think healthcare
systems are realising more and more that an integrated care model is the best for patients.
Having physicians coming and going is not compatible with this trend.
Hmm, that's interesting. I would have expected you to start with staffing shortages, which
as a problem plaguing all areas of health care. I mean, general physicians have been
trying to raise awareness for several years about the dramatic rise in their case loads.
Well, yes. Short staffing is definitely a challenge for nurses in any setting,
but particularly hospitals. And this affects profession in a number of ways.
For example, nurses may not feel like they are doing enough, causing dissatisfaction and burnout.
It can certainly be emotionally and physically draining when repeatedly you can't provide
the care you think is necessary.
This can lead to significant turnover in many healthcare organisations and settings.
Also, most concerning is the fact that staffing issues are a hindrance to patient safety.
Recent research shows that nursing shortages result in errors as well as higher morbidity
and mortality rates.
Hmm, and I would imagine that staffing shortages would lead to longer working hours, is that
true?
Yes, that is true.
Nurses often work extended hours in overtime, which puts them at risk for making mistakes.
A recent survey showed that 47% of nurses reported working regular overtime.
What is your organisation's policy on this?
Do you think that regular overtime is acceptable?
You know that nurses should not work more than 40 hours a week, and we believe they
should work no more than 12 hours in a day, ideally less, because you reach a point where
you start to have cognitive decline. It also creates situations where nurses start to treat
each other poorly.
What are some challenges that nurses face that people might not be aware of?
I would have to say workplace violence and bullying and harassment, a report that came
out last year from the Government Accountability Office found that healthcare workers in inpatient
facilities such as hospitals experienced high rates of non-fatal injuries such as hitting,
kicking and beating.
Nurses also regularly experienced bullying and harassment.
The report I just mentioned found that 71% of nurses said that they had been harassed
by a patient, which is far lower than the percentage reported by physicians.
That is the end of Part C. You now have two minutes to check your answers.
[Unclear interval — replay the original audio.]
That is the end of the listening test.
